facts.statement: The genus name Aetodactylus means "eagle finger" and it belongs to the Targaryendraconia group of pterosaurs.
facts.quote: Aetodactylus (meaning "eagle finger") is a genus of targaryendraconian pterosaur.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was discovered in 2006 by Lance Hall near a construction site in Mansfield, Texas.
facts.quote: This specimen was found in 2006 by Lance Hall near a construction site in Mansfield, near Joe Pool Lake

facts.statement: Timothy S. Myers named the genus Aetodactylus in 2010.
facts.quote: Aetodactylus was named by Timothy S. Myers of SMU in 2010.

facts.statement: The type species A. halli was named to honor the discoverer, Lance Hall.
facts.quote: The type species is A. halli, named in honor of the discoverer.

facts.statement: The holotype lower jaw measures 38.4 cm in total length, with the symphysis (where the halves join) accounting for 15.8 cm.
facts.quote: The jaw SMU 76383 is 38.4 cm long, 15.8 cm (~41%) of which is joined left and right jaws.

facts.statement: The fossil preserves evidence of 27 pairs of teeth, with the surviving teeth described as pointed, slightly curved backward, flattened, and slender.
facts.quote: 27 pairs of teeth were present; the two remaining teeth are pointed, curved slightly backward, flattened from side to side, and slender.

facts.statement: Unlike related genera like Anhanguera and Ornithocheirus, Aetodactylus lacks a bony crest on its lower jaw.
facts.quote: Unlike some other ornithocheirids, such as Anhanguera, Coloborhynchus, and Ornithocheirus, there is no bony crest on the lower jaw.

facts.statement: Fossils of Aetodactylus were found in the Tarrant Formation, a marine sandstone dating to approximately 97 million years ago during the middle Cenomanian.
facts.quote: The rock it was found in is a calcareous marine sandstone rich in mud–sized particles, from the middle Cenomanian-age (approximately 97 million years old) Tarrant Formation.

facts.statement: Aetodactylus lived approximately 98 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous in what is now the United States.
facts.quote: que vivió hace 98 millones de años en el Cretácico Superior en lo que hoy es Estados Unidos, Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Aetodactylus is distinguished from other ornithocheirids by features such as an expanded anterior jaw, a strongly compressed symphysis, evenly spaced teeth, and an upward curve of the lower jaw.
facts.quote: Aetodactylus is differentiated from other ornithocheirids by several anatomical details of the lower jaw, including the slight expansion of the anterior end of the lower jaw, the strong vertical compression of the symphysis, the relatively constant spacing of the teeth, and the slight upward curve of the lower jaw.

facts.statement: While originally thought to be related to Boreopterus, later analysis placed Aetodactylus closely related to Cimoliopterus.
facts.quote: Aetodactylus was considered a possible relative of Boreopterus in the original description, but subsequent cladistic analysis found it to be closely related to Cimoliopterus instead.

facts.statement: Aetodactylus represents one of the earliest known ornithocheirids.
facts.quote: Aetodactylus representa uno de los primeros ornitoqueiridos.

facts.statement: The time range for Aetodactylus is estimated between 100.5 and 93.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Cenomanian (100.5 to 93.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: Aetodactylus is notable for being one of the youngest definitive records of the ornithocheirid family.
facts.quote: Aetodactylus represents one of the youngest definitive records of ornithocheirids.
